turns.zh: 我猜在那个同心圆流程里有很多“提出异议并承诺执行”。有没有你发现的、关于这个 PRFAQ 过滤过程里异议和承诺的数量、告诉你也许这不是个好想法？

turns.speaker: Bill Carr
turns.en: Not necessarily. So I'll tell you partly also why the Fire Phone happened was, from my point of view, I think that we had had a number of successful products where, in some cases, there were a lot of people who doubted whether it would work. A lot of people inside Amazon doubted that the Kindle was going to be a good idea. I remember contentious board meetings on this topic. So even within a company that was considered innovative, you would have a lot of people that would doubt things. I can tell you that for years is working on Prime Video, I would tell people about what our envision was of you watching on your TV set and we're going to have our own motion studio. We'll make our own movies and TV shows. And they would laugh at me. They thought that was crazy. So that's not necessarily the sign of whether the product is right or wrong. And so that's a problem actually, that makes it harder to know.
turns.zh: 不一定。所以我告诉你部分原因 Fire Phone 发生，是，从我的视角，我觉得我们之前有几个成功产品，有些情况下很多人怀疑它会不会 work。亚马逊内部很多人怀疑 Kindle 会是个好想法。我记得在这个话题上有过 contentious 的董事会会议。所以即使在一个被认为创新的公司里，你会有很多人怀疑东西。我可以告诉你，多年做 Prime Video，我会告诉人们我们的愿景是你在电视上看、我们要有自己的摄影棚。我们会做自己的电影和剧。他们会笑我。他们觉得那疯了。所以那不一定是产品对错的迹象。而那其实是个问题，让它更难知道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And I think something Amazon's incredibly good at is being okay with a lot of failures, and I think that's part of the reason there's been so much innovation. Is that true?
turns.zh: 对。而我觉得亚马逊极其擅长的一点是：对很多失败感到 ok，而我觉得那是这么多创新的部分原因。是真的吗？

turns.speaker: Bill Carr
turns.en: I'd say it's partially true. I mean, again, it's hard for me to do a compare and contrast with other companies. But I can tell you did we have a lot of things that we launched that failed? Yes. Some of them are very public and obvious. I'll give you one that people don't really realize. It's something called... We had a feature in the early 2000s called Slots. And what it was was it was basically third parties could bid on different search terms and put a little ad in there.
turns.zh: 我会说部分对。我的意思是，再次，很难和其他公司做比较。但我能告诉你：我们发布了很多失败的东西吗？是的。有些非常公开和明显。我给你一个人们没真意识到的。有个东西叫……我们在 2000 年代初有个功能叫 Slots。它基本是第三方可以对不同搜索词竞价、在里面放个小广告。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds familiar.
turns.zh: 听起来耳熟。

turns.speaker: Bill Carr
turns.en: Well, obviously, that works now on Amazon, but it didn't work then because we simply didn't have the scale that Amazon has today. So a lot of times a product idea, a perfectly good idea, you just have the wrong time or the technology isn't there. I mean, Jeff wrote about a product that was a puck that sat in your kitchen that you would talk to and ask it for things and could shop from it. He wrote about that in 2004. Well, the technology wasn't there to be able to create that little puck, which one day would become Echo. It was a decade away. But we had a lot of things we launched that failed. We were not afraid to take what we considered a well-calculated risk. I think many, many companies are less willing to do so, less committed to product innovation, and really do not want that fear of... They do fear failure, and they're really focused on their near-term financial goals. It's not their fault. It's the way a public company and Wall Street interact with each other creates this dynamic.
turns.zh: 对，显然，那现在在亚马逊 work 了，但当时不 work，因为我们根本没有今天亚马逊的规模。所以很多时候一个产品想法、一个完全好的想法，你只是时机不对、或者技术还没到。我的意思是，Jeff 写过个产品，是个放在你厨房、你能和它说话、让它帮你找东西、能从它购物的小圆盘。他在 2004 年写过那个。好，当时技术还造不出那个小圆盘——它有一天会变成 Echo。那是十年后的事。但我们发布了很多失败的东西。我们不怕承担我们认为计算过的、好的风险。我觉得很多很多公司更不愿意那么做，对产品创新承诺更少，真的怕那种……他们确实怕失败，而且真的聚焦在近期财务目标。不是他们的错。是上市公司和华尔街互动的方式创造了这个动态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to pull on that thread a little bit more. It feels like a lot of companies talk about, "We're okay failing. We're okay launching things that don't work," but then in practice, their performance review is impacted. Teams get shut down, budgets get pulled. Is there something that you recommend to companies that want to actually improve in this? What could they actually change and actually do this well?
turns.zh: 就顺着这条线再拉一点。感觉很多公司说“我们对失败 ok。我们对发布不 work 的东西 ok”，但实践中，他们的绩效评估受影响。团队被关掉，预算被抽走。你有没有建议给真正想在这方面改进的公司？他们能真改变什么、并真做好这个？

turns.speaker: Bill Carr
turns.en: Yeah, I just spoke with actually a senior executive at a well-known Silicon Valley company about this topic the other day and said, "Well, what is it we had structurally at Amazon, especially from a people point of view, that would enable or encourage people to take these risks?" Because, yes, in a lot of companies, if you go work on the project that fails, then your career is in the garbage can and/or your compensation system, you're going to lose out on that bonus. So there were two things. One was our compensation system. So there were no performance bonuses. So if I was running the book business and I had a killer year from a financial point of view, there was no extra kicker for me. And if I ran the book business and it had a bad year, there was no financial penalty for me either because our compensation was based on the stock price. (01:11:12): So we all had an incentive to do what was right for the company, frankly, over a long-term because trying to win off of short-term fluctuations off Wall Street is a losing proposition, which meant that therefore, if I am... Because I had that situation, I moved off of working on our largest P&L, and then the book business and music and video business, now I'm going to go work on digital media. There is zero business there. This might not work. Well, my compensation didn't change as a result of that. It didn't change one way or the other. We tended to also have a performance management system that then would change compensation based on evaluating what did you actually deliver more in an input method. We cared about the outputs too, but just there are plenty of people that could be-
turns.zh: 对。其实我前几天刚和一个知名硅谷公司的高管聊这个话题，我说：“好，我们在亚马逊结构性地、尤其从人的角度，有什么能赋能或鼓励人们承担这些风险？”因为，对，在很多公司，如果你去做那个失败的项目，那你的职业生涯就进垃圾桶了，和/或你的薪酬体系，你会丢掉那笔奖金。所以有两件事。一是我们的薪酬体系。没有绩效奖金。所以如果我管图书业务、从财务角度过了个杀手级年份，对我没有额外 kick。而如果我有图书业务、过了个坏年份，对我也没有财务惩罚，因为我们的薪酬基于股价。(01:11:12) 所以我们全都有激励去做对公司长期对的事，坦白说，因为试图从华尔街的短期波动里赢是个输的命题，那意味着：因此，如果我是……因为我有那个情况，我从我们最大的 P&L——图书业务、音乐和视频业务——移开，现在我要去做数字媒体。那里零业务。这可能不 work。好，我的薪酬并没因此改变。它没朝任何一边变。我们也倾向于有个绩效管理体系，然后会基于评估你实际交付了什么、用更输入的方式改变薪酬。我们也 care 输出，但只是有很多人可能——

turns.speaker: Bill Carr
turns.en: Just, there are plenty of people that could be in a business that's up and to the right but has nothing to do with them. And so we tried to focus more on, well, what did you actually build and contribute, ways you improved selection or lowered prices, or whatever that might be. So those two things about the compensation mattered a lot. And then the second thing was having a CEO who was really committed to it and it wasn't something that they delegated to someone else. (01:12:31): So Safi Bahcall, I think, writes about this in his book Loonshots, where part of the conditions that are necessary for innovation to occur are that you actually create different structures of decision-making, of approvals, of all kinds of things, if you create some team that's going to go build something new and innovative. Because most of the structures inside a big company are designed to crush and impede a small innovative team that's trying to go build something new. They need speed, but approval here, approval there, it's going to get in their way. (01:13:10): We solved that two ways, one was when we went to go build digital media and AWS, we put two of our smartest leaders in the company on those things, Steve Kessel and Andy Jassy. And number two, they were meeting with Jeff regularly. Jeff was deeply engaged with them, reviewing what are we going to go build? Part of the decision to decide where we're going to go build. And so he could then also, between their seniority and of course him being the CEO, they could run interference on these sorts of things too. So even if you want to have innovation, even if you really do crave it, you're willing to take the risk, if you don't set up the organization in the right way, you're just not going to get it.
turns.zh: 只是，有很多人可能在一个一路向上的业务里、但那和他们毫无关系。所以我们试图更聚焦：好，你实际建了什么、贡献了什么，你改善选择或降价的方式，或 whatever。所以那两件关于薪酬的事很重要。然后第二件事是：有个真的 committed to it 的 CEO，而且不是他们委派给别人的事。(01:12:31) 所以 Safi Bahcall，我觉得，在他的书《Loonshots》里写了这个，创新发生所需的必要条件之一，是你真为要去建新而创新的东西的团队，创造不同的决策结构、审批结构、各种东西。因为大公司里大部分结构是用来压碎和阻碍一个小创新团队的。他们需要速度，但这里批一下、那里批一下，会挡他们路。(01:13:10) 我们两种方式解决：一是当我们去做数字媒体和 AWS，我们把公司最聪明的两个领导放在那些事上——Steve Kessel 和 Andy Jassy。二是他们定期和 Jeff 开会。Jeff 深度参与他们，评审我们要建什么。部分决定我们要去建哪。(01:13:10 续) 所以他也能——凭他们的资深和他们当然是 CEO——为他们跑干涉（run interference）。所以即使你想有创新，即使你真渴望它、愿意承担风险，如果你没用对的方式设组织，你就是得不到它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I'm glad we got into that, I wasn't planning to talk about that and I'm glad we did. Final topic, this concept of Bar Raisers, it feels like it's been such a core way of allowing Amazon to scale successfully, and I think that's something a lot of people can implement, it's a very one-off thing you could just implement at your company. Can you just talk about what this idea of a Bar Raiser is in the hiring process and then what people can do if they wanted to add this to their hiring process?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我很高兴我们进到那个，我本来没计划聊那个，但很高兴我们聊了。最后一个话题，Bar Raiser 这个概念，感觉它是让亚马逊成功扩张的核心方式之一，而且我觉得那是很多人能落地的、一个你能就在你公司实施的、很独立的东西。你能讲讲招聘流程里 Bar Raiser 这个想法是什么，然后人们如果想把这个加到他们招聘流程能做什么？

turns.speaker: Bill Carr
turns.en: So the Bar Raiser hiring process is a process, it was actually one of the first ones that was established and published, pretty early in the company's history back in 1999. And we created it for a simple reason, to quote one senior leader at Amazon, "We had new people hiring new people hiring new people." We were in our hyper-growth phase, okay? The company was only, what, three, four years old, and we were growing like a weed at that point. (01:14:47): So this started off actually in our tech org, and what our senior leaders in tech realized is, my gosh, we hire some new engineering leader, and then the next thing is that their job is to go hire the senior managers, and they'll go hire managers. And all these people have been here for a week, so they don't really even know our company yet, they don't know our culture yet, they don't know our standards yet. So what information are they using to make these hires, and what information they were using is obviously they were just using their own personal judgment, and their personal judgment combined with whatever criteria they used at prior companies that they worked for. So let's say if they came over from Microsoft, if Microsoft had some methodology or criteria, they probably would just apply that. (01:15:38): Well, is that methodology or criteria relevant to our company? Because every company has a different culture, and I'm here to tell you that if someone's been a super successful vice president at Microsoft, does not mean they could be as super successful at Amazon or at Google or Facebook. Sometimes they can, but these companies are very different, they all do work very differently. The way leadership happens and decisions are made are very different. So how do we fix this problem other than letting it run rampant and basically hire a bunch of people who are, we don't know if they fit our culture and we don't know if they fit our high standards we have for what we expect of engineering leaders or engineers? (01:16:21): So they created this Bar Raiser process, which by the way, they borrowed from Microsoft, which had a process called As Appropriate. And the concept was that on every interview loop there's one person, who is not the hiring manager, who doesn't report to the hiring manager, who's not the recruiting manager, they're in the business, they're a software development manager, or they're a marketing manager, and they are on the interview loop and they're a Bar Raiser, which means when we get to the debrief meeting, they will run that meeting, not the hiring manager, not the recruiter, they will run the meeting. And it also means that they technically have veto power over the hiring manager, which, by the way, a good Bar Raiser never uses, or I never saw a Bar Raiser use. I was a Bar Raiser, and in my 15 years at Amazon I never used it, never saw it used. (01:17:14): And then finally, which actually was not true in 1999 but later became true, was once we established our leadership principles, we created a set of objective criteria that would be used and an interview methodology that would be used in every interview, which was the objective criteria would be our leadership principles, and the methodology would be behavioral based interviewing. (01:17:33): So this Bar Raiser basically would be a subject matter expert on how this process worked, they'd conduct the debrief to make sure that we were actually adhering to the process, that people were sticking to the objective criteria rather than saying, "I don't think we should hire this person because, I don't know, they don't seem to want to work here enough." Maybe that's a valid reason, but it's actually not part of our objective criteria. And so the Bar Raiser was there to act as a balance also on the urgency bias that every hiring manager has, which is like, I got to fill these roles, but rather than filling them with the next warm body they find, make sure they fill them with people who actually meet our standards, fit our culture and meet our standards for functional excellence too.
turns.zh: Bar Raiser 招聘流程，是个流程，它其实是最早建立并发布的一个，在公司历史很早的 1999 年。我们创建它有个简单理由，引一位亚马逊高管的话：“我们在让新人招新人、新人招新人。”我们在超增长阶段，好？公司才三四年大，那时我们像野草一样长。(01:14:47) 所以这其实始于我们的技术组织，我们的技术高管意识到：天，我们招了个新工程领导，然后接下来他的工作是去招高级经理，他们会去招经理。而这些人全都才来一周，所以他们甚至还不了解我们公司、不了解文化、不了解标准。所以他们用的是什么信息做这些招聘？他们用的显然只是他们自己的个人判断，加上他们在之前工作过的公司用的任何标准。所以假设他们从微软过来，如果微软有某种方法或标准，他们大概就直接套用。(01:15:38) 好，那方法或标准对本公司相关吗？因为每家公司文化不同，而我来告诉你：如果有人在微软是个超级成功的副总裁，不意味着他能在亚马逊或谷歌或 Facebook 同样超级成功。有时能，但这些公司很不同，运作方式很不同。领导发生和决策做出的方式很不同。所以我们怎么修这个问题，而不是任它泛滥、基本招一堆我们不知道合不合文化、不知道达不达我们对工程领导或工程师的高标准的人？(01:16:21) 所以他们创造了 Bar Raiser 流程，顺便说，他们从微软借的，微软有个叫 As Appropriate 的流程。概念是：在每一个面试 loop 里，有一个人，不是招聘经理、不汇报给招聘经理、不是招聘经理，他们在业务里，是个软件开发经理、或市场经理，而他们在面试 loop 里、是个 Bar Raiser，也就是当我们到复盘会（debrief），他们主持那个会，不是招聘经理、不是 recruiter，他们主持。而且它意味着他们在技术上有对招聘经理的否决权——顺便说，一个好的 Bar Raiser 从不用，或我从没见过 Bar Raiser 用。我是个 Bar Raiser，在亚马逊 15 年里我从没用过、从没见过它被用。(01:17:14) 然后最后，其实 1999 年不真对、但后来变成对的，是我们一旦建立了领导力准则，我们创造了一套客观标准，会在每次面试用，面试方法也是在每次面试用——客观标准会是我们的领导力准则，方法是基于行为的面试（behavioral based interviewing）。(01:17:33) 所以这个 Bar Raiser 基本是这个方法怎么运作的主题专家，他们会主持复盘，确保我们真遵守流程，人们守住客观标准，而不是说“我觉得我们不该招这个人，因为，我不知道，他们似乎不够想在这工作。”也许那是有效理由，但它其实不是我们客观标准的一部分。所以这个 Bar Raiser 也在那作为对每个招聘经理都有的“紧迫感偏差”的平衡——像，我得填满这些角色，而不是用他们找到的下一个活人填满，确保他们用真达到我们标准、合我们文化、也达到我们职能卓越标准的人填满。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a cool process. Two questions along these lines, one is who has the final decision in hiring, is it the hiring manager?
turns.zh: 这么酷的流程。顺着这个两个问题，一是招聘里谁有最终决定，是招聘经理吗？

turns.speaker: Bill Carr
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this is just off advice from the Bar Raiser?
turns.zh: 而这只是 Bar Raiser 的建议？

turns.speaker: Bill Carr
turns.en: Yeah, so this often gets confused. The decision maker is the hiring manager, the whole interview loop and the Bar Raiser are actually just there to help the hiring manager make the right decision. Now oftentimes the hiring manager could feel like this is actually a bureaucratic process and a group of people that I have to sell and they're just in my way between me and hiring this person, which is kind of a natural feeling to have. (01:18:54): But one of the feedback I would always give managers who are new to this is like, no, no, no, that's not the way to think about it, think about these people are helping you, because the amount of time you're going to put into the hiring process may seem like a lot, but if you hire the wrong person, boy, that amount of time you're going to have to deal with managing that person, that's going to be a lot more, the impact on the team, impact on you. So making a great decision here is important, they're here to help you. (01:19:20): So yes, the final decision is with the hiring manager, technically speaking the Bar Raiser could block them from a decision to hire someone, but they would, well done they would help the hiring manager see the reasons not to hire the person through a Socratic method and how they would guide the discussion.
turns.zh: 对，所以这常被搞混。决策者是招聘经理，整个面试 loop 和 Bar Raiser 其实只是帮招聘经理做对的决定。现在常常招聘经理会觉得这是个官僚流程、一群我得去推销的人、他们只是我和招这个人之间的挡路石，那是一种自然感觉。(01:18:54) 但我总给新经理的反馈是：不不不，别那么想，想这些人在帮你，因为你投入招聘流程的时间可能看起来很多，但如果你招错人，天，你要处理管那个人的时间会多得多，对团队的影响、对你的影响。所以在这里做个好决定很重要，他们在这帮你。(01:19:20) 所以对，最终决定在招聘经理，技术上 Bar Raiser 能挡住他们招某人的决定，但他们——做得好——会用苏格拉底式方法、引导他们讨论，帮招聘经理看到不招那人的理由。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then when you're choosing a Bar Raiser, is there any suggestions you have of who to choose and how often you pull them into these things? Because it could also be a huge time suck.
turns.zh: 然后当你选 Bar Raiser，你有没有建议选谁、多久拉他们进这些事一次？因为它也可能超耗时。

turns.speaker: Bill Carr
turns.en: It is a huge time suck, and it sometimes could be up to 10 hours of my week spent actually as a Bar Raiser. The selection process is you start with, as a company, I would recommend if you wanted to do this, you'd pick a department to pilot it with. Pick people who are A, care a lot about your hiring process, B, appear to be good interviewers, and C, seem to have high standards. It's also a great role for people who are earlier in their career by giving them this additional leadership opportunity. It's a great way to grow and develop leaders, by the way, because this added responsibility is a great way for them to start testing out leadership. And you have to train them properly and you have to have dedication to the process, but I generally would try to pilot it within one group at first.
turns.zh: 它是超耗时，有时我一周多达 10 小时花在当 Bar Raiser 上。选择流程是：你从，作为公司，我建议如果你想做这个，选一个部门去 pilot。选这样的人：A，很 care 你的招聘流程；B，看起来是好面试官；C，似乎有高标准。对更早职业生涯的人，这也是个好角色，给他们这个额外的领导机会。顺便说，这是成长和培养领导者的好方式，因为这个额外责任是他们开始试领导力好方式。而且你得 properly 训练他们、得对流程有 dedication，但我一般会先试着在一个组里 pilot。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One last question before we get to our very exciting lightning round. Many people are listening to this, they're considering implementing some of these things, trying to figure out how to actually make these real. If someone were trying to move along the path of becoming more Amazonian, which of these elements and processes do you think often has the most impact? And/or is there something fundamental that needs to change to allow for some change like this to happen at a company, in your experience?
turns.zh: 进很刺激的快问快答前最后一个问题。很多人在听这个，他们在考虑落地其中一些、想办法怎么真让它们成真。如果有人试图走在变得更 Amazonian 的路上，这些元素和流程里你觉得哪个常常最有影响？和/或，凭你的经验，有没有什么根本的东西需要改变、才能允许这种改变在公司发生？

turns.speaker: Bill Carr
turns.en: Yeah, good question. And the first thing I'd say is one thing to be careful of is a lot of times when I'm talking to a company about these processes they say, well, does this mean we need to turn into Amazon? And first thing I tell them is, well, first of all, I couldn't turn you into Amazon if I wanted to, because you have your own culture. And secondly, no, that's not the idea is for you to try to become Amazon, the purpose is to sort of look at these processes and best practices they have and consider adopting parts or all of them into your organization to improve these, every company of a certain scale has these same processes, so this is just a different way to do them. So you should have scalable, repeatable processes for each one of these, pick one, here's one choice of ways to do these things. (01:21:58): The other piece of advice I give is that a lot of these changes are relatively profound, they really require buy-in all the way up to the CEO, if you're really going to change the way you do product development, or if you're really going to change the way you do hiring, that probably requires buy-in of the CEO, and so I would seek to get that probably before I would move too fast. Some of these things, though, can be piloted in your own little group, like your one little product development group. You want to decide you want to start writing PR FAQs, you probably can decide to do that. But again, try to check with your leadership. (01:22:32): The other thing I would just tell you is that for any of these processes, these in our book, or any book, implementing a new process is not easy. And if you go into it lightly and dip your toes into it and try it out, it's probably not going to work for you, because it'll be hard at first, and it requires some level of commitment to actually work through that hard part and say, I'm really committed to doing this, and it will take a few months for you to get good at it. So you have to have commitment and discipline to get through it. Anyone can really do these things, it just requires commitment and discipline.
turns.zh: 对，好问题。我第一件要说的小心点是：很多时候我和公司聊这些流程，他们说，那是不是意味着我们得变成亚马逊？我第一件告诉他们的是：首先，就算我想，我也没法把你变成亚马逊，因为你有你自己的文化。其次，不，那想法不是让你试图变成亚马逊，目的是看这些流程和最佳实践、考虑采纳部分或全部进你的组织来改善这些——每个到一定规模的公司都有这些相同流程，所以这只是做它们的不同方式。所以你该为每个都有可扩展、可重复的流程，挑一个，这里是个做这些事的选择。(01:21:58) 我给的另一条建议是：很多这些改变相对深远，它们真需要一路到 CEO 的 buy-in，如果你真要改变你做产品开发的方式、或真要改变招聘方式，那大概需要 CEO 的 buy-in，所以我会寻求先拿到那个，再走太快。不过有些事能在你自己小群里 pilot，像你一个小产品开发组。你想决定开始写 PR FAQ，你大概能决定做那个。但 again，试着和你的领导核对。(01:22:32) 我还会告诉你的是：对任何这些流程，我们书里的、或任何书里的，落地新流程都不容易。如果你轻轻进去、把脚趾探进去试一下，它可能不 work，因为一开始难，而且它需要某种程度的承诺去真熬过那难的部分、说“我真的 committed 做这个”，而且你要好几个月才能擅长它。所以你必须有承诺和纪律熬过去。任何人都能真做这些事，只是需要承诺和纪律。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And in our chat we've basically just scratched the surface of a lot of these things, if people want to dig deeper there's obviously your book Working Backwards, which we'll link to in the show notes. I know you also work with companies to implement a lot of these practices. Could you just talk about what it is you can help folks with and then how to potentially engage if they're interested?
turns.zh: 而在我们的聊里我们基本只是抓了这些事的表面，如果人们想挖更深，显然有你的书《Working Backwards》，我们会在 show notes 里链。我知道你也和公司一起落地很多这些实践。你能讲讲你能帮人们什么、然后如果他们有兴趣怎么潜在接洽？

turns.speaker: Bill Carr
turns.en: Sure, great. Yeah, Colin, and I, one of the reasons we wrote this book was to pass on what we learned to the next generation of business leaders at scale with a book, but also because we had a passion to work with companies directly one-to-one. And so we are advisors, consultants, call it what you will, but non-traditional, we don't have a team of people working for us. Each of us just work directly with the companies who engage us. (01:23:55): And generally speaking what we do is the right kind of company for us to work with, first of all, has to achieve a certain scale. Companies that are in the product market fit phase, they need to focus on getting product market fit, they probably don't really need to focus much on how they put in scalable, durable processes. Like sure, some of these could definitely be helpful to you even if you're in that phase, but really these are designed for, my company's become complex now, I've got multiple product lines, it's well over 100 million in annual run rate, growing fast, complex. So most of our clients are either large, well past series C private companies, or they're public companies. And in most cases, a C-level leader, or the CEO themselves, has read our book and recognizes that they have a lot of the same problems that we had at Amazon, and looks at these as useful solutions and wants us to help them implement them. (01:24:56): So we tend to usually first actually go in and do an assessment of how they do things today, because to help people move from one place to another we have to understand where they are, and then we come up with a prioritized list along with that, the CEO and C-level leaders, of what are the things that would be most useful, what are the symptoms and problems you're having and what are the root cause solutions that could be found in these processes? And then we sort of prioritize those and come up with a plan to work within the organization to help them implement those. And what's also different is that we're very hands- on working at all levels of the company, and as we do it we will be there in the meetings with the teams to help coach them and teach them along so that we make sure that it actually gets implemented properly and to spec, and they get to the outcome they want.
turns.zh: 当然，好。对，Colin 和我，我们写这本书的原因之一，是用一本书把学到的传给下一代商业领导者、规模化，但也因为我们有激情直接和公司一对一工作。所以我们是顾问、咨询，随你怎么叫，但非传统，我们没有团队为我们工作。我们各自直接和接洽我们的公司工作。(01:23:55) 大体上说我们做的、对我们合适的公司，首先得达到一定规模。在 PMF 阶段的公司，他们需要聚焦拿 PMF，他们大概不太需要聚焦怎么放可扩展、持久的流程。当然，有些这些即使你在那阶段也肯定对你有帮助，但这些真为“我的公司现在变复杂了、我有多个产品线、年 run rate 远超 1 亿、增长快、复杂”而设计。所以我们多数客户要么是大、远超 C 轮的私公司，要么是上市公司。而且在多数情况下，一个 C 级领导、或 CEO 自己，读过我们的书、认识到他们有很多和我们在亚马逊时同样的问题，把这些看作有用的解决方案，想让我们帮他们落地。(01:24:56) 所以我们通常先真的进去、评估他们今天怎么做，因为要帮人们从一个地方移到另一个，我们得理解他们在哪，然后我们和 CEO 及 C 级领导一起，想出个优先列表：什么最有用、你有什么症状和问题和什么是能在这些流程里找到的根本原因解决方案？然后我们排那些的优先级、想出个计划在公司内工作、帮他们落地那些。而且不同之处是：我们非常 hands-on 在公司各级工作，而且我们做时会在会议里和团队一起、帮 coaching 他们、教他们，确保它真被 properly 落地、按规格，他们到达想要的结果。

turns.zh: 所以在管理世界，不意外，《Good to Great》。我会说《Drucker on Management》，或 Drucker 的《The Effective Executive》。然后另一个我说有点不同的是我会推荐 Steve Jobs 传记。我从没在 Apple 工作过，但看那个弧线，很多那些事运作的方式和我在亚马逊经历的没那么不同，所以它是个好窗口，看在一个经历产品创新和大幅增长的公司、科技公司里是什么样。在个人层面，近期的书会是 Neal Stephenson 的《Seveneves》是个最爱，还有《A Gentleman in Moscow》。

turns.speaker: Bill Carr
turns.en: Yeah, it's actually quite basic, it's tell me about your most significant professional accomplishment. And I have to always clarify this, by this I mean not some award you won or some promotion you got, I mean something you built, or some product, some process, some organization you built, something like that. And I could basically then, once they get into that example, ask a lot of probing and follow-up questions and I could fill an entire hour interview just sticking with this one example to really understand how they... Using the STAR method, which is to try to understand everything from the situation to the result, and everything they did in between, who they influenced, how they'd influenced, what decisions they had to make, what roadblocks they encountered. If I just pull on that one string I can learn a whole lot about a candidate.
turns.zh: 对，它其实挺基础，是“跟我说说你最重大的职业成就”。而我总得澄清这个：我意思是不是说你得的某个奖、或某个升职，我意思是你建了的东西，或某个产品、某个流程、某个你建的组织，那种东西。然后我基本能在他们进那个例子后，问很多探究和跟进问题，我能用这一个例子填满整整一小时的面试，去真理解他们怎么……用 STAR 方法，也就是试图理解从事情到结果的一切，和他们之间做的所有事，他们影响了谁、怎么影响的、他们得做什么决策、遇到什么路障。如果我只是拉那一根线，我能学到关于一个候选人一大堆。

turns.speaker: Bill Carr

Most people confuse speed with velocity, and the difference between the two is that velocity has both speed and a vector to it, meaning there's some specific destination. And so I see a lot of people who are going very, very fast, but the destination isn't very clear, they haven't really thought that out well. So slow is smooth, smooth is fast.
turns.zh: 好，一个我在职业上、也在某种程度个人上常回到的，是“慢就是顺、顺就是快”（slow is smooth and smooth is fast）。这个，我相信起源其实是海军陆战队侦察狙击手，所以不是要推广那个特定手艺，但它的点是：其实，我们在亚马逊大量这么做，很多时候，要真快，你得先慢、对你做什么和要去哪非常清楚。多数人把速度和速率（velocity）搞混，两者区别是速率既有速度又有方向向量，意思是某个具体目的地。所以我看到很多人走得非常非常快，但目的地不清，他们没真想透。所以慢就是顺、顺就是快。
